context_title:
Build a single-file Python application named main.py that runs a production-grade HTTP server and exposes a full “autonomous app builder agent” system powered by the glm-5 model. The server must include (1) a JSON + multipart API, (2) a streaming SSE API compatible with OpenAI-style chat.completion.chunk events, (3) a complete web UI inside the same app for controlling the agent, viewing files, running builds, and previewing the running app, and (4) a Nix-based build/runtime pipeline that can produce runnable, deployed preview instances. The implementation must be fully functional, complete, unabridged, production-ready, and must not contain placeholders, mocks, stubs, dummy logic, or simulated outputs. Every feature described below must be implemented end-to-end.

System requirements to implement (from scratch, end-to-end):
	1.	Runtime and packaging constraints

	•	Implement everything in a single Python file: main.py.
	•	The server may generate, read, and write project files for the apps it builds inside per-session workspaces on disk, but the platform code itself must remain in main.py.
	•	The UI must be served by the same server process and implemented either as embedded HTML/CSS/JS strings or as on-the-fly generated static assets, but still driven from main.py.
	•	Provide a deterministic startup path: environment variables configure secrets, DB, quotas, and build tools.
	•	The agent must support extended autonomous sessions (multi-hour, long-horizon) with durable state, retries/backoff, and resumability through persisted checkpoints and logs.  

	2.	Core product goal: autonomous full application creation

	•	Implement an “agent run” workflow that takes a user product specification and produces a complete runnable application (frontend + backend + tests + build configuration + run command) in a per-session workspace.
	•	The agent must be able to produce applications in multiple programming languages, at minimum: Python, Node.js, Go, Rust, Java, .NET, and PHP.
	•	For each generated project, the system must produce a Nix-based build/run configuration that is actually used to build and run the project.
	•	The agent must be fully autonomous: it plans tasks, edits files, installs/builds dependencies via Nix, runs tests, runs the app, performs browser-based verification, fixes failures, and repeats until it meets acceptance criteria or until explicit safety/time limits are reached.  

	3.	System architecture: manager/editor/verifier with orchestration and durable runs

	•	Implement a hierarchical agent architecture with three internal agent roles that all use glm-5 but with role-specific system prompts and strict responsibilities:
a) Manager (Planner): decomposes the user spec into an executable plan, defines milestones, acceptance criteria, test strategy, and decides which tool actions occur next.
b) Editor (Builder): performs concrete code changes and project scaffolding steps; proposes file edits as structured patches; runs builds; updates configs.
c) Verifier (QA): runs automated checks; executes test suites; launches a preview; conducts headless browser flows; validates UX and critical paths; produces bug reports and minimal diffs for fixes.  
	•	Implement a run manager that executes agent runs as durable workflows:
	•	Only one active run per session at a time.
	•	Steps are persisted in a database so a run can continue after transient failures or server restarts.
	•	Each step supports retries with exponential backoff and hard caps.
	•	Every step produces structured artifacts (logs, diffs, screenshots, videos) and a concise summary that is fed back to the Manager agent rather than raw logs.  

	4.	Decision-time guidance (DTG): dynamic micro-instruction injection

	•	Implement a “decision-time guidance” mechanism that monitors tool outputs (stderr, build logs, test failures, HTTP errors, repeated loops) and injects short corrective micro-instructions into the next model call without rewriting the entire base system prompt.
	•	Implement DTG as:
	•	A lightweight rule + classifier pipeline that maps signals to guidance labels.
	•	A curated library of micro-instructions per label (e.g., “You are stuck repeating the same change; change strategy”, “A dependency error occurred; inspect lockfile and Nix config”, “UI test failed; reproduce with browser automation and capture artifacts”).
	•	A gating policy that limits frequency and size of guidance to preserve stable prompting and reduce cost.

	5.	Reversible workspaces: checkpoints, rollbacks, and auditability

	•	Implement per-session workspaces rooted under a server-controlled directory with:
	•	Git initialization inside each workspace.
	•	A checkpoint system that snapshots: files, key metadata, run state, and any lightweight project state needed to revert quickly.
	•	Rollback capability: if a run step introduces regressions or breaks build/run, the system can automatically revert to the last good checkpoint and continue from there.
	•	Implement checkpoint storage as content-addressable snapshots: store manifests and immutable chunk objects (or a functionally equivalent mechanism) to allow fast fork/rollback semantics rather than only linear overwrites.

	6.	Nix-based build and run pipeline with fast/full modes

	•	Implement a build subsystem that uses Nix to provide reproducible environments and builds for generated projects.
	•	Implement two build modes and enforce their use:
	•	Fast mode: incremental iteration, cached environment, optimized for short feedback loops.
	•	Full mode: hermetic verification build, used before declaring success, before packaging artifacts, and before final preview promotion.  
	•	Implement caching/bypass logic for environment provisioning by persisting computed environment exports to a cache file and validating it against the current store before reuse; if invalid, rebuild environment.
	•	The agent must be able to modify Nix configuration when needed (add dependencies, add language toolchains) and then trigger rebuilds, while preserving reproducibility.

	7.	Tool layer: strict, auditable tool actuation inside sandboxes
Implement an internal tool API (not exposed to external users directly) that the agent uses via tool calling. Each tool must: validate inputs, log every action, enforce resource limits, and run in an isolated sandbox. Implement at minimum these tools:

	•	File tools
	•	Read file, list directory, write file (atomic), apply unified diff patch, delete/move file, search text, compute project tree summary.
	•	Command execution tool
	•	Run commands in the workspace with timeouts, CPU/memory limits, and restricted environment variables.
	•	Capture stdout/stderr, exit codes, wall time, and structured summaries.
	•	Support streaming logs to the UI during long operations.
	•	Nix build tools
	•	Fast build and full build commands, with clear result objects and deterministic logs.
	•	Preview runner
	•	Launch the built app, allocate a port, expose an internal preview URL, and health-check it.
	•	Track process lifecycle and kill/cleanup on completion or failure.
	•	Headless browser test tool
	•	Use Playwright (or equivalent) to open the preview URL and execute user-flow tests automatically created by the Verifier agent.
	•	Collect screenshots and video recordings, plus console logs and network errors.
	•	Return a structured test report and artifacts.  
	•	Artifact tool
	•	Store and retrieve artifacts (logs, diffs, reports, screenshots, videos) by run ID and step ID, with metadata in DB and files on disk.

	8.	Closed-loop “build → preview → browser QA → patch → re-test”
Implement the main autonomous loop as a deterministic state machine:

	•	Input: user spec + optional files.
	•	Manager produces: plan with milestones, acceptance criteria, language choice (or polyglot), architecture decision, and an initial project blueprint.
	•	Editor executes: scaffolding + code generation + dependency setup + Nix config.
	•	Tool step: fast build; if fails, DTG guidance triggers targeted repair; loop until fast build passes or rollback triggers.
	•	Tool step: run unit tests; if none exist, create real tests; tests must run and must be meaningful for the app’s core features.
	•	Tool step: preview run; health check.
	•	Verifier executes: generate Playwright flows based on acceptance criteria; run headless tests; collect artifacts.
	•	If failures: Verifier produces a minimal bug report + patch plan; Editor applies patch; loop back to fast build and tests; then rerun browser QA.
	•	Finalization: full build; full test pass; browser QA pass; produce a release artifact (zip/tar) and a human-readable run report.  

	9.	APIs: external endpoints for chat, streaming, sessions, agent runs, and artifacts
Implement the following HTTP endpoints with strict validation and consistent JSON error formats:

	•	Health
	•	GET /api/health returns server ok, model default, DB status.
	•	Chat (LLM gateway for non-agent usage)
	•	POST /api/chat supports JSON and multipart with files; returns reply, reasoning (if provided), and tool_calls (if any).
	•	POST /api/chat/stream streams SSE in OpenAI chunk format.
	•	Agent UI and control plane
	•	GET /agent serves the agent control web UI.
	•	POST /api/agent/sessions creates a new session with metadata.
	•	GET /api/agent/sessions/<id> returns session state.
	•	POST /api/agent/sessions/<id>/upload accepts files to seed the workspace.
	•	POST /api/agent/sessions/<id>/run starts an autonomous run from a spec; returns run id.
	•	GET /api/agent/runs/<run_id> returns run status, steps, summaries, and current plan.
	•	GET /api/agent/runs/<run_id>/stream streams run progress events as SSE (distinct from model streaming) including step starts/ends, logs, diffs, preview URL changes, test results, and final outcome.
	•	GET /api/agent/runs/<run_id>/artifacts lists artifacts; GET /api/agent/artifacts/<artifact_id> downloads artifact content.
	•	GET /api/agent/sessions/<id>/files lists workspace tree; GET /api/agent/sessions/<id>/files/<path> reads file; GET /api/agent/sessions/<id>/diff returns latest diff since last checkpoint.
	•	POST /api/agent/sessions/<id>/rollback rolls back to a checkpoint.
	•	Security and limits
	•	All endpoints must enforce request size limits, file count limits, per-IP rate limits, and authenticated access where configured.

	10.	Web UI inside the same app (separate interface)
Implement a fully functional web interface at /agent that allows:

	•	Create/open sessions.
	•	Enter a product spec and start a run.
	•	Stream live progress: current plan, current step, console logs, build output, test output.
	•	Browse and open generated files with syntax highlighting.
	•	View diffs between checkpoints.
	•	View preview URL in an embedded iframe (or a link if embedding is blocked).
	•	View browser test artifacts: screenshots and video playback.
	•	Download final packaged artifact.
	•	Trigger manual actions: stop run, resume run, rollback, rerun verification.

The UI must not rely on external assets/CDNs; serve all assets from the same server process.
	11.	Database: Postgres persistence with Neon-compatible TLS settings

	•	Implement Postgres persistence with robust connection pooling and retry.
	•	Store: sessions, runs, steps, tool invocations, model calls, costs/latency, artifacts metadata, checkpoints manifests, and audit logs.
	•	Ensure schema migrations run on startup safely.
	•	Ensure graceful shutdown closes pools.

	12.	Model integration: glm-5 agent with tool calling

	•	All model calls must use the BigModel/OpenAI-like chat completions interface with glm-5 as default.
	•	Support tool calling end-to-end:
	•	Define tool schemas.
	•	Parse tool_calls and execute tools.
	•	Feed tool results back to the model as tool messages.
	•	Persist full traces.
	•	Implement deterministic prompting:
	•	A stable base system prompt for each agent role (Manager/Editor/Verifier).
	•	DTG micro-instructions appended as a separate system message segment without duplicating system prompts.

	13.	Safety, isolation, and governance

	•	Implement sandboxing for all command execution and preview processes with:
	•	Strict timeouts and resource caps.
	•	Network egress controls (deny by default; allowlist configurable).
	•	Secret handling: never write secrets to generated project files; pass them only via runtime environment injection when explicitly required.  
	•	Implement a hard “autonomy budget”: max wall time per run, max steps, max tool invocations, max retries, max browser runs, and max artifact storage.

	14.	Output requirements for the model generating the system code
When implementing this system, output must include:

	•	The complete main.py file in full, unabridged, production-ready code.
	•	Any additional files strictly required at runtime must be embedded or generated by main.py on startup, not delivered as separate source files.
	•	No explanations, no summaries, no ellipses, no placeholders, no TODOs, no mock logic, no incomplete branches.
	•	All endpoints and UI must function end-to-end and be runnable as-is with environment variables set for API keys and Postgres.

Implement the above system exactly, in full, as a cohesive platform where the glm-5 agent can autonomously create complete applications, build and run them via Nix, verify them with headless browser QA, self-fix failures with DTG-driven guidance, and expose a separate agent UI inside the same server.
